Memory Map

This document describes how the computer divides its 16 MiB address space among RAM, expansion memory, CL-GD5428 video memory, I/O devices, and firmware. Return to the main page.

The revision 2.1 address specification is frozen. This document may be corrected or expanded without a new revision. Any change to an address range, slot assignment, register address, or privilege attribute requires a new memory map revision.

Revision 2.1 extends revision 2.0 by assigning I/O slot 11 to the IDE interface and processor interrupt level 2 to its interrupt request. Revision 2.0 firmware remains compatible but cannot use IDE until it installs the new register and interrupt support. Revision 2.0 introduced the privilege model. Each range now carries a privilege attribute, and the hardware enforces it. User-mode code cannot reach the I/O region or the firmware EEPROM, and a cycle that tries ends in a bus error. Main memory goes further: every user-mode cycle in $000000-$3FFFFF passes through a page table, so a program reaches only the 4 KiB pages the BIOS mapped for it. Section 2 gives the rules, Bus and Address Decode gives the protection circuit, and Paging gives the page unit.

BIOS scratch memory moves from $3F0000-$3FFFFF to physical $000000-$01FFFF, which returns the top of DRAM bank 1 to applications and puts the exception vectors inside BIOS territory. The unimplemented regions $A00000-$DFFFFF become the page-table aperture, I/O slot 10 holds the page-unit control block, and SYSREG2 holds the VGA window grant. Revision 2.1 assigns I/O slot 11 to a two-device parallel ATA interface. Every other address range, slot assignment, and register address carries over from revision 2.0 unchanged.

1. Main Memory Map

The top 2 MiB of the address space contains I/O devices and the firmware EEPROM. Each remaining region is 2 MiB wide.

Complete 24-bit address space
Start End Size Function Notes
$000000 $1FFFFF 2 MiB DRAM bank 0 Physical frames 0 through 31 hold the exception vectors and BIOS private memory, and the BIOS never maps them into a user context. The boot ROM alias replaces the first 128 KiB until the firmware disables the overlay. User-mode cycles anywhere in the bank are translated.
$200000 $3FFFFF 2 MiB DRAM bank 1 The second 2 MiB DRAM bank. Revision 1.2 reserved its last 64 KiB for the BIOS; revision 2.0 does not. User-mode cycles are translated, and a logical page in either bank can map to a frame in either bank.
$400000 $5FFFFF 2 MiB Expansion slot 1 memory Fixed EXP_MEM2_n window for front slot 1.
$600000 $7FFFFF 2 MiB Expansion slot 2 memory Fixed EXP_MEM3_n window for front slot 2.
$800000 $9FFFFF 2 MiB CL-GD5428 VGA host-memory window Mapped one-to-one onto the CL-GD5428 linear display-memory aperture. The board has 2 MiB of video RAM, so the window is fully populated. Supervisor only until the BIOS writes SYSREG2, which grants it to the running program.
$A00000 $BFFFFF 2 MiB Page-table aperture, entries 512 through 1023 EXP_MEM5_n selects the page unit. Entry N appears at $A00000 + (N - 512) * 4096. Supervisor only.
$C00000 $DFFFFF 2 MiB Page-table aperture, entries 0 through 511 EXP_MEM6_n selects the page unit. Entry N appears at $C00000 + N * 4096. Supervisor only.
$E00000 $FFFFFF 2 MiB I/O and firmware Divided into sixteen 128 KiB slots, listed below. Supervisor only, with no exception.

2. Privilege and Protection

Every range in the map carries a privilege attribute. The motherboard reads FC2, which the MC68EC000 drives high for supervisor cycles and low for user cycles, and refuses a user-mode cycle that addresses a supervisor-only range. The refused cycle reaches no device and the processor takes a bus-error exception.

Application code therefore reaches hardware only by calling the BIOS, which runs in supervisor mode. The circuit is in Bus and Address Decode and the call gate is in Firmware ROM.

Privilege attribute of each range
Start End Contents User-mode access
$000000 $3FFFFF Main memory Translated. A page is readable, writable, or refused according to its table entry
$400000 $7FFFFF Expansion slot memory windows Allowed
$800000 $9FFFFF CL-GD5428 host-memory window Refused unless the BIOS has granted the window
$A00000 $DFFFFF Page-table aperture Refused
$E00000 $FFFFFF All sixteen I/O slots, the system registers, and the firmware EEPROM Refused

The two refused regions follow the bits the decoder already tests, so the protection decode is two address comparisons: A23..A21 = 100 and A23..A21 = 111. Main memory needs no comparison at all, because the page table answers for every page separately. The page unit refuses user-mode access to its own aperture.

VGA Window Grant

The display would be unusable if every pixel needed a BIOS call, so the BIOS can open the host-memory window to the running program by writing $01 to SYSREG2 / VGAGRANT and close it again by writing $00. A board reset closes it. The CL-GD5428 control registers in I/O slot 3 stay supervisor only, so display mode, pitch, and banking remain BIOS decisions.

Page Table

Main memory is divided into 1024 pages of 4 KiB. Each context has its own table of 1024 entries, and the hardware holds 32 contexts at once, so a context switch is a single register write. An entry carries a physical frame number, a valid bit, and a writable bit. Paging defines the format, the aperture, and the control registers.

Supervisor cycles are never translated. The BIOS sees flat physical memory, which is how it reaches the vector table, its own working memory, and any frame it is about to hand to a program.

What Protection Does Not Cover

The page unit relocates and isolates; it cannot page on demand. The MC68EC000 bus-error frame does not support instruction continuation, so a faulting access cannot be repaired and retried. Every page a program uses stays resident, and a fault ends the program.

Keeping firmware frames out of user tables is a BIOS rule rather than a hardware interlock. Nothing in the hardware stops the BIOS from mapping frame 0 into a user context, and doing so would hand that program the exception vectors.

3. BIOS Private Memory

Physical $000000-$01FFFF, frames 0 through 31, belongs to the firmware. It holds the exception vector table, the supervisor stack, and BIOS working state. User-mode code reaches it only if the BIOS maps one of those frames into a context, which the BIOS must never do.

BIOS private region
Start End Size Function
$000000 $0003FF 1 KiB MC68000 exception vector table
$000400 $01FFFF 127 KiB BIOS stack and working state

Keeping the vector table out of every user table is what makes the rest of the scheme hold. A user-mode program that cannot address frame 0 cannot rewrite a TRAP vector to point at its own code, so the BIOS entry points are the only way into supervisor mode.

The range sits inside DRAM bank 0, so it shares that bank's refresh and initialization rules, and the boot ROM alias covers it until the firmware disables the overlay. Firmware must start DRAM refresh, finish memory initialization, disable the overlay, write its vector table into RAM, and build at least one page table before it leaves supervisor mode.

4. I/O and Firmware Map

The final 2 MiB of the address space is divided into sixteen 128 KiB slots. A slot can contain a device, firmware, or space reserved for later use. Every slot is supervisor only, including the two that reach the expansion connectors, so the register maps below describe what the BIOS sees rather than what an application may touch.

I/O and firmware slots from $E00000 through $FFFFFF
Slot Start End Size Device Purpose and connection
0 $E00000 $E1FFFF 128 KiB MC68901 MFP Provides the UART, timers, interrupt controller, GPIO, and PS/2 keyboard interface. Its 24 canonical registers occupy odd addresses $E00001-$E0002F on the lower data byte.
1 $E20000 $E3FFFF 128 KiB Intel 82077AA-1 Controls two Mitsumi D359M3D drives. Eight canonical host locations occupy odd addresses $E20001-$E2000F on the lower data byte.
2 $E40000 $E5FFFF 128 KiB Yamaha YMF262 OPL3 Provides FM synthesis. Its registers use the lower 8-bit data lane. Four canonical ports occupy $E40001-$E40007.
3 $E60000 $E7FFFF 128 KiB CL-GD5428 VGA I/O registers Provides the host-side interface to the CL-GD5428 registers. VGA I/O port P appears at $E60000 + P. A16 is not decoded, so the 64 KiB port map repeats once in the upper half of the slot. See CL-GD5428 VGA.
4 $E80000 $E9FFFF 128 KiB System control registers Controls the boot ROM overlay and the VGA window grant, and leaves room for future motherboard controls and status registers.
5 $EA0000 $EBFFFF 128 KiB MC6850 MIDI ACIA Provides the MIDI serial interface on the lower 8-bit data lane. Its primary registers are at $EA0001 and $EA0003.
6 $EC0000 $EDFFFF 128 KiB Expansion slot 1 I/O Fixed IO6_n window for front slot 1.
7 $EE0000 $EFFFFF 128 KiB Expansion slot 2 I/O Fixed IO7_n window for front slot 2.
8 $F00000 $F1FFFF 128 KiB DS1285 RTC Provides the real-time clock and battery-backed CMOS RAM. Its 64 canonical byte registers occupy odd addresses $F00001-$F0007F on the lower data byte and repeat every 128 bytes. See DS1285 RTC.
9 $F20000 $F3FFFF 128 KiB MC68230 PI/T Provides three parallel ports and a 24-bit timer. Its 32 register selects occupy odd addresses $F20001-$F2003F on the lower data byte. See MC68230 PI/T.
10 $F40000 $F5FFFF 128 KiB Page-unit control Selects the active context at $F40001 + 2C and turns translation off and on at $F40041 and $F40043. Write-only, value encoded in the address. See Paging.
11 $F60000 $F7FFFF 128 KiB Parallel ATA IDE interface Provides one 40-pin cable for two ATA or ATAPI devices. The command block starts at $F60000, and the control block starts at $F60010. See IDE Interface.
12 $F80000 $F9FFFF 128 KiB Reserved Available for future I/O.
13 $FA0000 $FBFFFF 128 KiB Reserved Available for future I/O.
14 $FC0000 $FDFFFF 128 KiB Reserved Available for future I/O.
15 $FE0000 $FFFFFF 128 KiB Firmware EEPROM The permanent firmware mapping.

5. CL-GD5428 VGA Byte Lanes

The CL-GD5428 expects little-endian byte ordering, while the MC68EC000 uses big-endian byte ordering. The host interface crosses the 16-bit data lanes: CPU D15..D8 connects to CL-GD5428 D7..D0, and CPU D7..D0 connects to CL-GD5428 D15..D8. The corresponding byte-enable connections are swapped with the data lanes.

The byte enables cross with the data. CPU /UDS drives CL-GD5428 SA0 and CPU /LDS drives CL-GD5428 SBHE*, so a byte at CPU address N reaches controller byte address N.

This wiring applies to the CL-GD5428 host-memory window and its I/O-register interface. It does not change either address range in the frozen memory-map specification.

6. Boot ROM Overlay

After a hardware reset, the firmware EEPROM also appears at the bottom of the address space so the CPU can read its reset vectors. Disabling the overlay reveals DRAM bank 0 at those addresses. The EEPROM remains available at its permanent high address throughout this process.

Devices visible in the boot and firmware address ranges
State Start End Visible device
Immediately after hardware reset $000000 $01FFFF Firmware EEPROM alias
After the firmware disables the boot overlay $000000 $01FFFF DRAM bank 0
Always $FE0000 $FFFFFF Firmware EEPROM

The CPU reads its initial stack pointer at $000000 and its initial program counter at $000004, both from the EEPROM alias. The program counter stored in ROM should point into the permanent high mapping, such as $FE0100. The firmware can then disable the low alias without hiding the code it is running.

Disabling the overlay reveals BIOS private memory rather than application memory, so the firmware writes its working vector table into $000000-$0003FF after the switch. Both the alias and the RAM behind it are supervisor only, so the exception vectors are never writable from user mode.

7. System Control Registers

The system control block uses odd addresses on the lower 8-bit data lane. Only the first three registers have functions, and the block is supervisor only.

Motherboard control and status registers in I/O slot 4
Address Register Function
$E80001 SYSREG0 / SYSCTRL Any write disables the boot ROM overlay.
$E80003 SYSREG1 / DEBUG Write-only 8-bit hexadecimal debug display register. The upper and lower nibbles are continuously shown on two internal seven-segment displays.
$E80005 SYSREG2 / VGAGRANT Write-only. D0 high opens the CL-GD5428 host-memory window at $800000-$9FFFFF to user-mode cycles; D0 low closes it. A board reset closes it. D7..D1 are ignored.
$E80007 SYSREG3 Reserved.
$E80009 SYSREG4 Reserved.
$E8000B SYSREG5 Reserved.
$E8000D SYSREG6 Reserved.
$E8000F SYSREG7 Reserved.

Lower-byte writes to SYSREG3 through SYSREG7 are acknowledged and ignored. Reads from this block and upper-byte-only accesses end in a bus error, and so does any user-mode access.

8. 8-bit Peripheral Addressing

The 8-bit peripherals connect to D7..D0 and use /LDS. As a result, consecutive peripheral registers are two bytes apart in the 68k address space and use odd addresses.

peripheral register N = BASE + 1 + (N * 2)

MC68901 MFP

The MC68901 occupies I/O slot 0 and connects to D7..D0. CPU address lines A1..A5 connect to register selects RS1..RS5. The 24 defined registers run from GPDR at $E00001 through UDR at $E0002F; the complete table is in MC68901 MFP. Because local address lines A16..A6 are not decoded, the 64-byte register block repeats across the slot.

Intel 82077AA-1 Floppy Controller

The 82077AA-1 occupies I/O slot 1 and connects to D7..D0. CPU address lines A1..A3 drive the controller's A0..A2 inputs. Reads and writes to the same address can reach different registers.

82077AA-1 canonical register addresses
Address Read Write
$E20001 Status Register A Undefined
$E20003 Status Register B Undefined
$E20005 Digital Output Register Digital Output Register
$E20007 Tape Drive Register Tape Drive Register
$E20009 Main Status Register Data Rate Select Register
$E2000B FIFO data FIFO data
$E2000D Reserved Reserved
$E2000F Digital Input Register Configuration Control Register

Address lines A16..A4 are not decoded, so this 16-byte register pattern repeats throughout the slot. Firmware uses the first copy shown above. The full circuit and programming rules are in Floppy Controller.

Yamaha YMF262 OPL3

The OPL3 exposes four ports at the start of I/O slot 2. All four accept writes; only port 0 accepts a read.

OPL3 port addresses
Address OPL3 port Read Write
$E40001 Port 0 Timer status Register-array-0 address
$E40003 Port 1 Bus error Register-array-0 data
$E40005 Port 2 Bus error Register-array-1 address
$E40007 Port 3 Bus error Register-array-1 data

CPU A1 and A2 drive YMF262 A0 and A1. The pattern repeats every eight bytes because A16 through A3 are not decoded. Firmware uses the canonical copy above. Upper-byte accesses and reads from ports 1 through 3 end through the motherboard timeout. See YMF262 OPL3 for the complete interface.

MC6850 MIDI ACIA

The MC6850 connects to D7..D0 and uses /LDS. CPU address line A1 drives the ACIA's register-select input, so reads and writes to the same address can access different registers.

MC6850 register addresses and operations
Address Read Write MC6850 RS
$EA0001 Status register Control register 0
$EA0003 Receive data register Transmit data register 1

The MC6850 occupies I/O slot 5. Address lines A16..A2 are not decoded, so the two-register pattern repeats every four bytes throughout the 128 KiB slot. Firmware uses $EA0001 and $EA0003 as the canonical copy. The complete interface is defined in the MC6850 MIDI design.

MC68230 PI/T

The MC68230P10 occupies I/O slot 9 and connects to D7..D0. CPU address lines A1..A5 connect to register selects RS1..RS5, so the 32 register selects land on odd addresses $F20001 through $F2003F. Address lines A16..A6 are not decoded, so this 64-byte block repeats throughout the slot. The complete register table is in MC68230 PI/T.

9. IDE Register Addressing

The IDE interface occupies I/O slot 11. CPU address lines A3..A1 drive ATA DA2..DA0, and A4 selects the command or control block. The data register uses a 16-bit word at $F60000. Command-block registers 1 through 7 use the lower byte at odd addresses $F60003-$F6000F. Alternate Status and Device Control share $F6001D in the control block.

Address lines A16..A5 are not decoded, so the 32-byte pattern repeats through the slot. Firmware uses the canonical first copy. The IDE register table gives each read and write function.

10. DRAM Organization

Two 2 MiB banks provide 4 MiB of system DRAM. Each bank uses four 1M x 4 devices to form the computer's 16-bit data width.

Physical DRAM banks
Bank Address range DRAM devices Width Capacity
0 $000000-$1FFFFF 4 x TMS44400DJ-70 (1M x 4) 16-bit 2 MiB
1 $200000-$3FFFFF 4 x TMS44400DJ-70 (1M x 4) 16-bit 2 MiB
Total system DRAM 4 MiB
